scenarios.setup: A beaker of ice on a hot plate with a digital thermometer and a digital scale.

tasks.prompt: Heat the ice until it completely melts. Predict what will happen to the total mass of the beaker.
tasks.expectedOutcome: Mass stays the same. The law of conservation of mass states that matter is neither created nor destroyed during a physical change.
tasks.anomalyExplanation: Students often confuse phase changes with 'losing' or 'gaining' matter. Evaporation or melting only changes the state, not the total amount of substance.

tasks.prompt: Boil the water until it turns to steam. Predict what will happen to the volume of the substance.
tasks.expectedOutcome: Volume increases dramatically. Gas particles are much farther apart than liquid particles.

scenarios.setup: Two unknown substances (e.g., salt and sugar) with a hammer, a magnet, a circuit, and a burner.

tasks.prompt: Test Substance A by burning it in the Bunsen burner. Predict whether this is a physical or chemical change.
tasks.expectedOutcome: Chemical change. Burning produces a new substance (ash, gas) and is irreversible.

tasks.prompt: Dissolve Substance B in water. Then evaporate the water. Predict whether the original substance will be recovered.
predictionOptions: Yes, the original substance will return
No, it has been chemically changed and cannot be recovered
tasks.expectedOutcome: Yes, the original substance returns. Dissolving is a physical change, even though it looks like the substance has disappeared.
tasks.anomalyExplanation: Dissolving is often mistaken for a chemical reaction because the solid disappears. Evaporation proves that the molecules of the substance are still present and unchanged.

scenarios.setup: A digital scale, three measuring cylinders with equal volumes of honey, water, and oil, and a large transparent container.

tasks.prompt: Weigh equal volumes of honey, water, and oil. Predict which liquid has the highest density.
tasks.expectedOutcome: Honey is the most dense, followed by water, then oil.

tasks.prompt: Pour all three liquids into the same container. Predict the order they will settle in, from bottom to top.
tasks.expectedOutcome: Honey sinks to the bottom because it is the most dense. Oil floats on top because it is the least dense. Water sits in the middle.
tasks.anomalyExplanation: This visual proof connects the abstract calculation of density (mass/volume) to a directly observable physical behavior. Students can see that density determines buoyancy.
